#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Belatedly continues the plan from #108074 to deal with the fallout from golang 1.17 changing the behavior of `net.ParseIP`/`net.ParseCIDR` to prevent CVEs.

The approach here is:
1. Make sure every IP-valued field is being validated with `validation.IsValidIP` (merged as https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122931), and every CIDR-valued field is being validated with `validation.IsValidCIDR` (merged as https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123174)
2. Tighten up the validation performed by those functions (see the changes to `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation/ip.go` in the commit `"Tighten up IP/CIDR validation"` for details.). This also tightens up the behavior of `IsValidNonSpecialIP` (formerly `ValidateNonSpecialIP`) to reject two cases that it missed before (broadcast and global multicast).
3. Fix up `pkg/apis/*/validation/` to not revalidate unchanged IPs/CIDRs on updates, so that existing objects with "bad" IPs/CIDRs can still receive unrelated updates.
4. Fix up `pkg/apis/*/validation/` to allow fixing otherwise-immutable IP/CIDR fields by replacing "bad" IPs/CIDRs with equivalent good ones.

(Logically, step 3 should have come before step 2, but the code in step 3 can't be fully unit tested until there exists a concept of "formerly valid but now invalid IPs". E.g., you can't test "it's possible to upgrade a service with an invalid ClusterIP from single-stack to dual-stack without having to fix the existing invalid IP" unless there are IPs that will pass `IsDualStackIPs()` but fail `IsValidIP()`.)

See also  #122549 which works on replacing the "sloppy" IP/CIDR parsers with a better API.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Maybe "Fixes #108074" but there is at least additional code cleanup required...

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Kubernetes is now slightly stricter about what values will be accepted as
IP addresses and network address ranges (“CIDR blocks”).

In particular, octets within IPv4 addresses are no longer allowed to have
any leading `0`, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values (e.g. `::ffff:192.168.0.1`)
are now forbidden. These sorts of values can potentially cause security
problems when different components interpret the same string as referring
to different IP addresses (as in CVE-2021-29923).

This tightening applies only to fields in build-in API kinds, and not to
custom resource kinds, values in Kubernetes configuration files, or
command-line arguments.
```

/kind cleanup
/kind feature
/kind api-change
/priority important-soon
/sig network
/sig apimachinery

- What happens if you have an existing object that violates the new validation?
- “core” refers to a particular API group (`""`) and that might not be what you meant. Hence the rewording away from “core”.

> * What happens if you have an existing object that violates the new validation?

Ah, yeah, I mentioned that in the PR description but not the release note.

For most types, you're allowed to leave the bad value in place when making updates to other fields, and you can even patch arrays containing bad values. (e.g. there's a test that if you have a service with `externalIPs: ["1.2.3.04"]` that you can change it to `externalIPs: ["5.6.7.8", "1.2.3.04"]`).

The big exception to this is Endpoints/EndpointSlice, where it didn't seem worth it since (a) almost all Endpoints and EndpointsSlices are generated by controllers and are 100% valid anyway, and (b) both types can potentially be very large and thus would require _lots_ of extra validation if we want to allow preserving existing invalid values. So the rule there is that you can modify labels and annotations and other stuff like that without fixing bad pre-existing IPs, but if you change the `Endpoints.Subsets[]` / `EndpointSlice.Endpoints[]` at all, then the whole thing has to validate as though it was a new object.

(It's possible that some or all of this will change before the PR merges.)

> * “core” refers to a particular API group (`""`) and that might not be what you meant. Hence the rewording away from “core”.

Otherwise, I think we ought to cover all of the detail in the changelog entry. It's potentially a breaking change, although as a cluster operator you had to be kind of noncompliant already to be affected.

@thockin It is ready for review, and (assuming people agree with it), merging.

The change in behavior is:
1. There is now a stricter definition of "valid" [for IPs](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122550/commits/b839f544665d952788d5fcad4baece0515560f07#diff-8a9487299ceecf614a80ec27a90e65be788ac575ebc4d46080d157a22640aea8R27-R48) and [for CIDR strings](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/122550/commits/b839f544665d952788d5fcad4baece0515560f07#diff-8a9487299ceecf614a80ec27a90e65be788ac575ebc4d46080d157a22640aea8R27-R48)
2. All newly-set IP/CIDR values in objects of all core API types must be valid according to the new criteria. Pre-existing invalid IP/CIDR values are allowed to remain unchanged.
3. Immutable IP/CIDR-valued fields containing invalid IPs/CIDRs can be updated to be the canonicalized form of their existing IP/CIDR. (eg, if you have `clusterIP: 172.000.000.001`, you can change it to `clusterIP: 172.0.0.1`, but it's still otherwise immutable and you can't set it to anything else; there is exactly one string that any immutable invalid IP/CIDR can be changed to.)

(Note that the commits are sort of in the wrong order and break things in the middle, because there's no way to test the "allow updates to objects with invalid IPs" commit without first creating the concept of "invalid IPs".)

A few possible open questions:
- Is it OK to change the validation for (newly-created instances of) old API types? Consensus before was "yes", because there are security issues associated with allowing the "bad" forms.
- Would it be better to add API warnings for a few releases before changing validation?
- Should we require IPv6 IPs to be in canonical form (lowercase, minimal 0s, etc)? There are generally no security issues with allowing non-canonical strings, but there are also not really any good arguments for letting users pass non-canonical strings, and if you require them to be canonicalized then you can compare/hash them as strings without needing to parse them first. (The PR currently _does not_ require canonicalization. And in particular, for existing API fields, since we have to deal with old objects with bad values anyway, it wouldn't win us much. Perhaps we should start requiring it for newly-added API fields in the future? (As Antonio did with ServiceCIDR.))
  - Should we accept, but warn about, non-canonical IPv6 IPs?
/retest

At this point in time, after 3 years that golang 1.17 https://go.dev/doc/go1.17 was released with the parsers problem https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/100895,  I don't know if is less painful to remove the band-aid completely in one shot and add a feature gate (deprecated) as escape hatch than having to do all these gymnastics , meaning the last 2 commits here can be replaced by a feature gate that still allows the old value if the user enables it

@thockin @liggitt

The fact that the golang change happened 3 years ago is irrelevant, because the entire point of 100895 was to hide that change from kubernetes users. From kubernetes's perspective, the change _still hasn't happened yet_. "Ripping the band-aid off" now would be equivalent to having never done 100895 in the first place, which is to say, it will break some existing clusters.

This PR is the thing we actually wanted to do 3 years ago, but never got around to.

If you're just concerned about having the messy "allow pre-existing bad values" code in tree, #108074 considers the possibility that we might eventually stop doing that (and repair existing ones on read), so I guess if we think we're likely to do that, I could try to isolate the relevant code a bit more to make it more obvious that it's temporary, and to make it easier to remove later. (But OTOH, are we _really_ likely to implement that?)
IIRC The problem with the CVE was related to golang clients consuming those IPs, after 3 years there are no golang clients affected, we validated at that time kubernetes was not impacted

> after 3 years there are no golang clients affected

No, we intentionally broke that assumption! All of core k8s (and much of "peripheral k8s") is [still using the broken pre-1.17 parser](https://github.com/kubernetes/utils/blob/master/net/parse.go#L23-L27). This means that if you have an API object with something like `podIP: 010.0.0.2` in it, that k8s code will parse that as "10.0.0.2", and non-k8s golang code will treat it as having no IP, and non-golang code will parse it as "8.0.0.2", resulting in different behaviors which can theoretically be exploited by an attacker, which is exactly what CVE-2021-29923 was about.

> we validated at that time kubernetes was not impacted

That's not correct and not even possible. Every piece of code (inside _or outside_ of core k8s) that looks at any IP-valued field of any k8s object is potentially impacted. Even if we actually had properly validated that core k8s wasn't impacted in 2021 (which [we didn't](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/126203/commits/30bc1b59d70de99412dbe9d8944ab07a3d587463#diff-c2324126e8fa925fee94137c7f127001cfffa3132c6eb7aa14f32e4c023ba64eR237-R240)), that doesn't mean nobody broke things between then and now, and it doesn't mean that third-party code reading k8s objects isn't impacted by the fact that we allow objects to contain IP addresses which we implicitly expect all clients to parse incorrectly.
Agree that we need to ratchet this in.  Unfortunately I am out of time before code-freeze this cycle to dig in more than superficially.  Can we put this on the docket for ASAP in the next cycle?

OK, I think this is ready now, though I rebased it on top of #128786 (the first 4 commits) to avoid merge conflicts later.

~The fact that we need to switch between legacy and strict validation at runtime, combined with the addition of some new fields since I first started thinking about this (like the DRA stuff and ServiceCIDR/IPAddr) made me decide that I needed to add optional flags to `IsValidIP`/`IsValidCIDR`, to avoid an explosion of very similar validation methods. So I did that. I'm not sure I like the way I did it. (Originally I used a bitfield, but that just felt so un-go-like/un-k8s-like that I redid it with a `...string` instead.)~

EDIT: changed this: I realized there's really no reason to support "strict parsing but allow non-canonical" for new fields, so now there's one set of parsing methods for legacy fields (which allow non-canonical values and currently allow leading 0s, etc but eventually won't), and another set of parsing methods for new fields.

`IsValidIP`/`IsValidCIDR` default to strict validation so that for newly-added fields, you can just call them with no arguments and they'll do the right thing.

issue_context.title: Deprecate IPs with Leading Zeros ( CVE-2021-29923 )
issue_context.body:
To summarize the situation:

1. Since golang 1.17 IPv4 addresses with leading zeros are considered invalid. #100895
2. Kubernetes decided to keep compatibility with stored data so it forked previous parsers to allow IPs with leading zeros. #104368
3. The rest of the Kubernetes ecosystem seems to prefer to use default parsers and consider that data invalid https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107552#issuecomment-1033137581

We are in a situation where users can have IPs with leading zeros in their API objects, but may not be able to use it because the CNI, DNS, Ingress, ... implementation doesn't consider it valid

The proposal is (quoting thockin) 

> How about something like:

> 1) Any new builtin APIs should use ParseIP/ParseCIDR (not sloppy) and we let validation fail.
> 2) For the places we know of (service, ingress, netpol, pod, node, ...) we set a condition like "AmbiguousAddressSyntax", log them, maybe a metric.
> 3) Allow updates to otherwise immutable fields as long as the IP adress is changing from a malformed value to a correct value.
> 4) Ship that in 1.24.
> 5) Warn that in 1.25 or 1.26 such IPs will be tolerated if they exist, but rejected for new usage.
> 6) Implement (5)
> 7) Warn that in N+1 or N+2 we will fix such IPs upon read, effectively purging them from k8s
> 8) Implement (7) and ship
> 9) Maybe put these updates in a repair loop, ship that, then eventually remove sloppy parsing entirely

_Originally posted by @thockin in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107552#issuecomment-1035630181_

I'm working for migrating Services IPs as part of
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-network/1880-multiple-service-cidrs

Wondering if maybe we need a KEP here, but...

1. There was clear consensus that we had to do something to keep accepting bad IP values already in etcd, but less consensus on bad values in other places:
   - Do we want to / are we allowed to tighten validation for IP/CIDR fields in all objects? If someone has a controller that tries to create Services with `clusterIP` values like `172.030.000.010`, are we OK with that controller breaking in some future release due to stronger validation? (I think consensus was that normally we would not do this, but since there are security implications, we're probably OK doing it here?)
   - What about for IPs outside of API fields? If someone is launching kube-apiserver with `--service-cluster-ip-range 172.030.000.000/16`, are we OK with that suddenly resulting in kube-apiserver failing to start after some future upgrade?
2. The CVE / sloppy-parsing-fire-drill was just about IPs with leading 0s, but there are other edge cases:
   - Rejecting IPv6-wrapped IPv4 addresses (eg `::ffff:1.2.3.4`), which shoud be treated as IPv4 but may be misinterpreted by some code (potentially leading to the same sorts of "smuggling bad values past sanity checks" problems as with leading 0s).
   - Rejecting CIDR values that have bits set after the mask length, which may be interpreted as IPs rather than subnets by some software (#94484)
   - Requiring IPv6 addresses to appear in canonical form (eg `1234::abcd`, not `1234:0:0:0:0:0:0:ABCD`) to prevent reapply loops in controllers (eg #114505 warns about this). (This is only a problem for IPv6; any IPv4 address that is valid according to the new rules is also canonical.)
   - Some API objects are currently validated with [`ValidateNonSpecialIP`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4706516100649bf5a92c780488ea53924239ad17/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L6545) which rejects loopback, link-local, etc, and we may want to do that more broadly?
3. Presumably we want to make sure that CRD validation of IPs/CIDRs gets updated to match apiserver validation. We may have less ability to phase in changes over time here.
4. (Random thing to keep in mind: `netip.ParseAddr` accepts some strings that `net.ParseIP` does not (eg `fe80::1234%eth1`) so we need to be careful to not accidentally change our validation semantics when we switch to that.)
